FROM GEORGETOWN.

Austin Presbytery in Session... Was Never More Prosperous.

Special Telegram to the Examiner.

GEORGETOWN, April 8.—The Presbytery of Austin met at Georgetown on Thursday, at 7 p.m. A large attendance of ministers and elders were present. Rev. W.B. Bloys, of Coleman City, was elected moderator, and Rev. McClelland, of Brownwood, secretary. Two new churches were reported organized; also a large increase of membership and attendance on public worship in various churches. There are no unemployed ministers and now no unsupplied charge in the Presbytery. The Presbytery never was so strong or working in such a flourishing condition as now.

The trucks for the Georgetown Hook and Ladder company arrived to-day from New Orleans.

JACK WHARTON.

His Sudden Death, Friday.

Special Telegram to the Post.

NEW ORLEANS, April 7.—United State8 Marshal Jack Wharton died suddenly at 5 p. m., in an apoplectic fit. At about 3 p. m. he went into the office of Surveyor of the Port Pinchback, in the custom-house, and was talking with T. B. Stamps, a colored man and local politician. He complained of having a headache and of feeling hot, and asked to have the window opened and laid himself down on the sofa. Stamps noticed a change in his face and called Pinchback. Wharton looked up to Pinchback and said: "I am gone," and went off in a fit. Physicians were summoned, but could do nothing. He lay unconscious for two hours and then passed away.

FROM TURNERSVILLE.

Crop Prospects and Current News Items.

TURNERSVILLE, April 7.—The crop prospects are somewhat improved. Wheat has suffered seriously from rust, but is now coming out. In some instances, however, it still looks very sickly. The best planters in this section estimate from present prospects, about half a crop of wheat and full oat crop. Corn planting is about done, and cotton planting progressing. Some corn is up and looking well.

It is currently reported here that Prof. A. K. Barmore, of Coryell City, is in a low state of health, and losing his reason. His father has been telegraphed for from Rockdale, and has arrived to see to his son's case. It is said that his father has fled an affidavit of his son's insanity. Prot. B has been in charge of the school at Coryell for a good white, and has many friends who very sincerely regret his mistrust, and hope for his speedy restoration to health.

Mr. W. K. Morley, of Morley Bros., Austin, is in town to-day. Business is extremely dull and the merchants blue.

Gatesville is having a good boom, several new buildings being now in process of construction. Some of our citizens expect to visit Waco on the 20th, one of whom I am which. A young Beltonite will probably lead to the altar soon, one of Turnersville's belles. Sheep are doing well this spring and sheep-raisers are jubilant. A Burglar Shot.
Dick Batsell, colored, who is wanted both here and in Sherman to answer for burglaries he committed, was shot last night in Stringtown by Police Officer Clapp, about 9 o'clock, and it is thought that he is mortally wounded. He is the party who burglarized Mrs. Carleton's residence of a lot of jewelry, which was subsequently recovered from a pawn-shop. The officers were unable to meet up with him until last night, and when he saw them, broke and ran for the brush, followed by Officers Clapp and Ed Cornwall, who overtook the fugitive, who resisted arrest, when the officer struck him a blow over the head with a pistol, falling him to the ground. As he arose he struck at the officer with a soda-water bottle, and seeing it gleam in the dark, the officer, mistaking it for a pistol, fired on him and at the same instant Batse'l staggered and fell, but recovering himself, he hobbled into the brush, crawling a part of the time on his hands and knees. They procured lights and searched in vain for him, but he could not be found. The brush is very dense and the ground very rugged at that point. Clapp shot at his body with a large Colt's pistol, which is likely to produce death. The search for him will be resumed this morning.

Cairo, April 12.—The Circassian officers arrested in connection with the plot to assassinate the minister of war numbered sixteen. Dissatisfaction at non-promotion actuated them.

St. Petersburg, April 12.—That Poland may be represented at his coronation the Czar has appointed ten Polish district Marshals. A district marshal has not existed in Poland since 1863.

Revolution in Hayti.

Havana, April 12.—A revolution began in the capital of Hayti on the night of the 26th of March. Gonaives, of Port au Prince, and son entered the movement. Martial law was proclaimed and President Solomon is preparing to march to Cape Hayti with 3,000 men.

Laud League Convention.

Washington, April 12.—Committees of the Land League convention on resolutions and organization were to-day appointed. John Boyle, of Boston, offered a resolution which recites the fact of the imprisonment of American prisoners in English jails, quotes the Land League and dispatches of Minister Low-

ell and calls upon the president to immediately recall Lowell and provides for the presentation of the resolution to President Arthur by a committee. The resolution was unanimously adopted amidist great applause. The committee on credentials reported 227 delegates present.

Two More of the Golden City's Victims.

Memphis, Tenn., April 12.—Two more bodies lost by the disaster were discovered this afternoon four miles below here. One has been identified as Robert Kelly, second engineer of the ill-fated vessel, who remained so calm at his post until the steamer had been made fast to the coal fleet. Fort Worth, Texas, April 12.—Saturday night Bill Jackson, a negro, broke into a room occupied by the 15 year old daughter of Mr. Henderson, who lives a mile and a half south of this city, and after choking her until she was insensible outraged her. "The Last Rose of Summer."

The Adams Express company received a telegram yesterday morning from the Pittsburgh and Fort Wayne train which left here at 9 o'clock the previous evening for the East, that a man had been found concealed in a box in the express car and had been handed over to the officers at Van Wert, Ind. He gave his name as John McAuley, of 191 West Monroe street. The box, which was provided with wire at the top and bottom to give ventilation, was labelled "The Last Rose of Summer," and the expressmen supposed it contained flowers, but when Mr. McAuley was found snugly ensconced in it, they fancied they had captured a robber. He had with him a supply of provisions sufficient to last six days, and from the information gleaned, it was concluded that the man had adopted this novel way of traveling to save the difference between the passenger and freight rates of fare, the latter having been prepaid to Philadelphia. It is understood that Mr. McAuley is about sixty-five years of age and in comfortable circumstances, but given to eccentricities which have often set his family on their wits' end. It is said that if he had succeeded in reaching the City of Brotherly Love in his box he intended to undertake a similar trip to Denver, Col. It was lucky for Mr. McAuley that this attempt to reach the Atlantic seaboard as an express package was discovered in the daytime, for if he had been found in the night the express messenger would have been likely to have peppered him with a revolver. It is to be regretted that the agent, after satisfying himself that the man in the box was harmless, did not allow him to proceed in his novel conveyance merely for the purpose of testing a man's powers of endurance for two days and a night for the purpose of evading the expense of a few paltry dollars, and in order to give the sleepy Philadelphia papers a sensation. But the gentleman's scheme was nipped in the bud, and the company may require him to prove his object was not robbery. —Chicago Tribune.

He claimed that he was unditted by reason of disability for the duties given him, and that the company's agent knew of that fact.

PITTSBURG, (Pa.,) April.—El Hanova Spring Hotel, at Hayville, was burned this morning. Loss, $138 000. Fortunately no boarders were in the house.

Wholesale Lynching of Cattle Thieves.

PUEBLO, Col., April 1.—Between 2 and 3 o'clock this morning a mob of sixteen men quietly took from the county jail two notorious cattle thieves, Phoebus and McGraw, and hung them to a tree on Santa Fe avenue, within 100 yards of the jail. There is an organization in the county known as the Cattle Growers Association, a branch of the State organization, and is composed of cattle growers for protection of their property. There is little or no doubt that the mob was composed of members of this organization. The lynchers next rode to a ranch ten miles miles away, surrounded the house and captured S. P. Chastine, Billy Chastine and Frank Owsley. Their hands were securely bound and they were put on horses and taken to a thick patch of timber and etrung up. There is but one of the gang left.

Discovery of a Great Pot of Old Money.

ST. LOUIS, April 1.—Two laborers, digging a drain on the premises of James E. Haggerty, on Collins street, to-day, unearthed a large pot tightly sealed which proved to contain a large amount of English sovereigns, American silver dollars and a lot of Continental currency. The money has not yet been counted, but there is probably from $20,000 to $30,000 of coin which is dated in the last century. The currency bears the date in 1777. The house was occupied by Montgomery Blair many years ago, but afterward passed into the possession of Samuel Gaty.

The Bodies on the Golden City.

MEMPHIS, April 1.—All hope of recovering the dead bodies from the wreck of the Golden City has been abandoned. No further attempt will be made until the river falls sufficiently to permit divers to work with some show of success.

NEW YORK, April 1.—The Herald's St. Petersburg dispatch says: Lieutenant Sonnowoff was shot this morning at Cronstadt, in the presence of the troops of the fortress. All other persons condemned at the recent Nihilist trial had their sentences commuted by the Emperor to an indefinite period of hard labor in the mines.

The Rowing Race Between Oxford and Cambridge.

LONDON, April 1.—In the race today the Oxford crew won by six boat lengths. The Cambridge crew was the first to come out on the river. They took the Middlesex side. The final betting was five to one on the Oxfords. The boats started at one minute past one o'clock. The Cambridges were the first to take water and immediately led by half a boat's length, but were caught and passed by the Oxford boat before fifty yards had been traversed. At the soap works, a mile and a half from the starting point, the Oxford crew were in the lead by three lengths. At Hammersmith Bridge, two furlongs further on, they were four lengths in front of the Cambridge crew, and off Cheswick Mall the latter seemed to be fairly done with. The Oxford crew finished in good form. They won as they pleased. The Cambridge men were exhausted at the finish and their rowing was irregular.

A QUIET LYRIC PARTY.
Sixteen Masked Cattle Dealers Hang Five Men to Trees in One Night
PUEBLO, Col., April 1 — W. F. Phoebus and A. W. J. McGraw, cattle thieves, were taken from the county jail here at 2 A. M., by a party of sixteen masked men belonging to the Cattle Drovers' Association, who received admittance on representing that they were Deputy Sheriffs with a prisoner and hanged them to a tree in Santa Fe avenue. The lynchers subsequently went to Reynolds' place on St. Charles road, ten miles from Pueblo, and surrounded the house.

There they took out S. D. Chastine, Barry Chastine and Frank Owsby and hanged them to trees near the house. At Pueblo they bound and gagged the jailer to prevent alarm and did the whole work so quietly as to raise no disturbance and they were all in their beds by morning, so that no trace can be found to any man who was away from home last night. They told the Pueblo jailer they selected this morning because of the incredulity of the people to-day to prevent the immediate success of any alarm.

TRUMAN DUNHAM, President of the Cleveland Linseed Oil Works, an old and honored citizen, was caught in machinery, March 30, and killed. He wss alone in the basement, where there was a large belt which runs the grinder; in some unkown way he was caught in the belt, carried into the machinery and the body shockingly crushed. Deceased had been trustee of the Cleveland water-works many years.

The following murderers were suspended on the 31st: Doc. Wright, colored, at Chatham, Va.; Al. Weisinger and Bill Ludlow, at Selma, Ala. At South Pueblo, Colo., W. T. Phebus and J. W. McGrew, eminent horse-thieves, were taken from jail and hanged by masked men. The vigilantes then rode to a ranch ten miles away, captured the Chastine brothers and an accomplice named Owsby, and strung them up in the adjacent timber. It is stated that but one of the gang is left as a sample, and a necktie is ready for him.
J. W. SHEEHAN, a young man stopping at the Metropolitan Hotel, Kansas City, Mo., was found dead in his room, March 30, having taken poison. The following note was found on the table: "My father's address is William Sheehan, North Walpole, N. H." Sheehan had a letter of recommendation from the Smith Refrigerator Manufacturing Company, of Michigan City, Ind., speaking of him as a sober, industrious man. It is supposed he took the dose in a fit of despondency, finding himself out of work and among strangers.

During a severe storm near Reading, Pa., April 2d, a number of persons sought shelter in a shed behind which a large water tank had been erected. The tank rested on a heavy stone wall, and was also supported by girders of heavy timbers, but the force of the wind was so great that the girders were twisted off, and the entire mass fell on the shed, crushing the people under it, and completely burying them in the debris. George Shelthorn, aged 45, and his daughter Rosa, aged 9, were crushed or smothered to death; Mrs. Shelthorn was terribly mangled, and will probably die, and Charles Shelthorn, aged 14, was badly injured. John Cruse, aged 18, was also killed, his head being mashed to a pulp. George R. Full, owner of the farm, was severely hurt about the head and had three ribs broken. Fred R. Neill and several others escaped with a few slight injuries. The storm raged furiously in other sections, barns were blown down, fences were leveled, and fruit trees greatly damaged.

CORNELIUS J. VANDERBILT, brother of William H. Vanderbilt, fatally shot himself at the Glenham Hotel, New York City, April 2d. From the time of the shooting until his death Vanderbilt was unconscious. Many friends of the dead man and members of his family were present when he passed away. The reason for the act given by his friends is that it was the result of mental derangement brought on by years of suffering from epileptic fits. No other cause could be given, as his financial affairs are said to be in a most prosperous condition.

LILLY and Hany, two Indian murderers, were recently shot dead at Okmulgee, Indian Territory. The spectators were nearly all Indians, mainly friends of the prisoners. There was no disturbance, scarcely a word being spoken from the time the criminals were led from jail until the sharp report of the rifles announced that their doom had been sealed and the law vindicated. They were found guilty of the murder of an Indian sixty years old who had been robbed by Lilly, and who was prosecuting him for the theft. The murderers professed to have been converted and united with the M. E. Church. They died expressing the hope of eternal life.

OFFICER JONES, of Kansas City, Mo., was fatally wounded, April 3, while attempting to arrest two negroes who had been charged with theft. The men started to run away, but one of them, Dick Harrington, was captured. As the officers were taking him to the Central Station they were overpowered by a mob, who took the prisoner and swung him off from the Bluff street bridge. As he went over he shrieked that he was innocent. One of the crowd fired a pistol shot, the rope was cut, and he fell a corpse to the track below. The mob quickly dispersed and no arrests were made. The other man was captured in Kansas City, Kan., and is now in jail.

Several Florida negro children buried a baby alive, intending to dig it out immediately; but they got to playing at something else, and forgot the infant for hours, leaving it to die of suffocation.

Eugene Webster caught his enemy, Stephen Tarbell, in a secluded place at Bedford, Mich., tied him fast to a board, and leisurely inflicted horrible torture by cutting him here and there with a knife.

For some time past the most vigorous measures have been taken for the destruction of the locust plague in Cyprus. In the belief of the authorities, fully seven-eighths of the whole quantity of locusts with which the island is infested have been destroyed.

The Figaro learns that Mr. Van Rysselberghe, who has found how to communicate at great distances telephonically on the ordinary telegraphic wires, is going to sell his discovery for $200,000 to the French Government. Mr. Cochery, the French Postmaster General, is much impressed with its importance.

A Second Advent camp meeting is being held at Denton, Texas, by people who believe that the second coming of Christ is at hand, and might be hastened by a proper demonstration of readiness to receive Him. They have gone so far as to prepare a tent for the Saviour's occupancy, with a handsome bed and other furniture.

There is a general disposition among the Mayors of cities just now to worry the gamblers. The chief magistrate of Milwaukee is among the latest and most zealous to join in the movement. In one of his raids, thirty-seven well-known and more or less respected residents were taken to court and fined from $10 to $50 for playing faro.

—Mr. R. Barrett Browning's unexhibited portrait of his father is to be at once engraved, says the London World, and the engraving published. The poet has been painted as often as any man living, and his son's is one of various readings. In features it will be found an excellent likeness, in expression perhaps a little sterner than the original as Mr. Browning's friends have the pleasure of knowing him.

—The municipality of Rome have resolved on the erection of a monument to Garibaldi on the Janicular Hill. A subscription list has been opened, which the city of Rome headed with a contribution of eighty thousand francs. Telegrams have been received from Naples, Palermo, and Milan announcing that the municipalities of those cities have severally voted a hundred thousand francs for the monument.

—The Boot and Shoemakers' Union of San Francisco copyrighted a "white labor stamp" for use in factories where no Chinamen were employed. A large majority of the public would thereafter buy no boots or shoes that did not bear this stamp. But the discovery has been made that, through the connivance of white wholesale dealers, the entire product of several Chinese shops has been stamped for the market.

—Capt. Hull of the Yale boat's crew says of their diet while training: "If any one wants pie he can have it. All he has to do is to order it. With dinner we take claret or English ale, according to taste. They take their meals together at a hotel, and pick their food at will from the regular bill of fare." The Harvard oarsmen are not indulged to the same extent, though they are not kept on the strict diet usually prescribed.

—The annual sun dance of the Ponca Indians is described as having a considerably civilized aspect this year. There were blankets instead of buffalo robes, paints from a drug store instead of dyes from herbs, ropes instead of rawhide strips, and glass beads in place of wampum. The savage character of the ceremony continued, however, unchanged, the principal rite consisting of lacerating the flesh in various ways.

Manager Jack Harris appeared on the stage with a cocked revolver in each hand, and announced that he would begin firing in two minutes unless quiet was restored. The row ceased, and the entertainment went on. The account mentions that an anteroom of this theatre is devoted to gambling, the games being brisk between acts, and that the actresses serve drinks in the auditorium when not on the stage.

Mr. Yeocum was transferred by his Bishop from the pastorate of the latter to that of the former. He immediately received a formal letter from the Bethel officers asking him to resign, and on going to preach his first sermon in the church he found a notice on the locked door that there would be no services. A society established in Austria for the benefit of the German schools of the empire is to acquire an abundant working capital by means of a voluntary tax which the students at the University of Vienna have agreed to impose upon their consumption of beer. Whenever one of them disposes of six glasses at a sitting he must, instead of taking a seventh glass, contribute seven kreutzers (about 4½ cents) to the fund of the society. There are 2,000 such students, and it is estimated that each of them on an average drinks his six glasses at least twice a week. This will give the society an income of nearly $10,000 a year.

The shooting of the negro Smith by Policeman Martinez, should bring to public attention the danger of arming the police;—a pistol in the hands of a policeman is as dangerous as in the hands of a cow boy,—perhaps more so. Martinez, thought because he was a policeman he had a right to shoot down a flying thief, and yet, had he killed his victim, he would have been guilty of murder and been entitled to the honor of pulling hemp at the public expense; as it is, he will be subject to a charge of assault with intent to murder.

A policeman has no greater right to use his pistol upon a fellow-man than any other person has. He must only use it in self defense, and then strictly under the conditions of any other unofficial person; in making an arrest the policeman is the aggressor and should be careful to only use more force necessary to perform his duty.
The only excuse for sheriffs and other officers carrying deadly weapons, is that they may possibly encounter desperate men, who carry arms and would resist peaceable arrest.

Negro Horse-Thief Lynched.
ATHENS, Ga., Feb. 14—A colored man named Smeal, living on Thomas Dillard's plantation, Gurney county, was suspected of stealing a horse. Last night a mob broke open the negro's cabin and whipped him until he confessed to the stealing and took the mob to where the stolen horse was tied in the woods. The mob then hanged the negro to a blackjack limb near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road, where the body was found hanging today.

Lumpkin Independent: "On Friday night of last week the tan yard of Mr. J. G. Singer was visited by some one and six sides of leather stolen from the vats. The leather was missed on Saturday, but the thief left no clue by which he could be traced. During the early part of the week suspicion rested upon Jim Jones, a well known colored shoe-maker of this place, and on Tuesday night a search warrant was obtained, and in the house of Jones the six sides were found and identified. During the search and before the leather was found, Jim walked out of the house and made good his escape. It is not positively known whether Jim stole the leather either or whether he bought it from some one else, as he did not stop to make any explanations, and is still at large. Jones came to Lumpkin from Columbus some five or six years ago. He was generally industrious, and by adding farming to his shoe-making had nearly completed the payments on a comfortable home and over a hundred acres of land. He leaves behind him a wife and several small children to look out for themselves."

Cedartown Advertiser: "In another column we give an interview with Capt. A. G. West on the subject of the probable extension of the Cherokee Railroad. While the Captain says as yet that the matter is one of uncertainty, yet it seems to us everything augurs favorably for the project. There is no use to attempt now to enumerate fully the advantages this road, if built, will in the end be to Cedartown and surrounding country. If, as Capt. West says, coal can be laid down here at $2.50 per ton there will not be a more favorable spot in Georgia for manufactories. The lowest figure at which Chattanooga has been enabled to procure coal is $3.50 per ton. Atlanta, with her Georgia Pacific, can do little, if any, better. The fields to be reached by this new line will be bountiful in yield and the quality is said to be excellent. The Cherokee company control about seven thousand acres of the richest of these fields. They lie mostly, if not all, in St. Clair county, Ala. After these are exhausted, should they ever become so, if not before, the road will be extended to Birmingham, from where the famous Warrior and Cahaba fields are easily reached. The advantage of narrow gauge in penetrating the coal fields will be apparent, for with easier facility the mines lying at difficult points among hills can be reached. The difference in expense of running the narrow and broad gauge will enable the former to make transportation for doing shipments much cheaper. Indeed, we are told that Captain West has said that with this proposed road he can lay coal down cheaper in Atlanta (by the aid of Colonel Cole, we suppose) than she can get from any other source."

THE OLD MAN'S MONEY. Rivalry for Possession of Which Caused a Murder. An Attempt to Rob a Missouri Pacific Train Last Night Frustrated. Kansas City Police, Getting Wind of the Affair, Arrest Four of the Gang. Marvelous Escape from Punishment of a Notorious Chicago Crook. Miscellaneous News of Crimes and Criminals.
NEWBUROH, N. Y., February 14. Jonah Tompkins, residing at Tilke's hill, eight miles from Cold Spring, was murdered yesterday by his brother-in-law, Curtis Christian. Early in the morning the men set out together to buy cows and in the evening Christian returned and announced to his wife he had murdered Tompkins, stating where the body could be found. He then attacked his wife, but was overpowered and fled from the house. A search was made and the body found where indicated with the head crushed in by a stone. The indications are that a terrible struggle took place. The murderer is not yet arrested and it is believed has committed suicide. Supposed rivalry regarding the father-in-law's property was the cause of the crime.

KANAS CITY, Mo., February 14. The contemplated robbery of the Missouri Pacific train, due here at 8:40 to-night, was frustrated by the Kansas City police. It seems that seven men, all notorious characters of this city, formed a plan for the contemplated robbery some three months ago, but the final arrangements were only completed a few days ago, and to-night was set as the time. The place where the train was to be stopped was about five miles east of here. The police got wind of the affair sometime ago and have carefully nursed it. At 4 o'clock this afternoon five officers proceeded to the spot where the robbery was to take place and concealed themselves. The robbers soon appeared on the ground and cautiously began preparations for their work. A pile of ties and railroad iron was piled at the side of the track which they intended to use to stop the train. The officers pounced upon them and took in four of them, three making good their escape. These the officers hope to corral yet to-night. On the gang were found a number of revolvers, shot guns, masks, and lancers. The names of the gang arrested are Jas. Nooman, Thos. O'Shea, Pat Hanley and Peter Speer. They admit that they intended to commit the robbery as charged and have given the officers full details of their plans, when it was conceived and how it has been worked up. One of the gang undoubtedly gave his comrades away to the authorities.

CHICAGO, February 14.—Johnny Lamb, who has been on trial once for the robbery of Jaffrey's store three years ago, and twice for the murder of Policeman Race after the robbery, the last trial having been in progress several weeks, was to-day acquitted. As he passed out of the jail a free man, the inmates gave him a great ovation. He is now the greatest hero of Chicago crooks.

The mystery attending the death of Lake Ransom at Hinsdale is still creating excitement. Dr. Fitch offers $1,000 reward and the trustees of the village of Hinsdale $500 reward for the arrest of the murderers. The doctors believe the case is murder, most other people believe in the suicide theory. Important developments are expected.

CANTON, O., February 14.—Last night, at Osanaberg, Lincoln Murphy was instantly killed by a playmate striking him in the breast.

REDBANK, N. J., February 14.—George McGrace, the negro accused of committing an indecent assault upon three little white girls, had an examination to-day before Justice Childs and was held for the term of the grand jury. It was feared the prisoner would be mobbed during the examination.

STANFORD, Ky., February 14.—John Carr (colored) was assassinated while playing with his children in his own home tast night. The assassin is unknown.

LEXINGTON, Ky., February 14.—John Atkins, a fellow prisoner in jail with the three Ashland murderers, says Ellis told him he had a further confession to make, implicating other persons and supposed to implicate Neil and Craft, already under sentence of death for the crime.

JACKSON, Miss., February 14.—A shooting affray occurred on Capitol street last night between Geo. Harrell and David Harrington, two high toned young men. Four or five shots were exchanged. Harrington was shot in the thumb, stomach and head and Harrell was badly wounded.

SAN ANTONIO, Tex., February 14.—Charles Bowers, a German blacksmith, Fred Douglass, S. Cook and a sub-contractor of the Sunset railway named Alen Murdock, were murdered for their money while asleep near Lampas, Mexico. All three were shot in the back of the head, and the murderers are therefore supposed to have been a' least three in number.

GALVESTON, February 14.—In an affray at Matamoras, Texas, between Col. Hernandez and Domingo Maino, an artillery man, the former shot and killed the latter.

LEXINGTON, Ky., February 14.—Ellis, one of the Ashland murderers in jail to-day, denies the story of Adkins that he (Ellis) said his confession implicating Neal and Craft is not true. He still still sticks to his first confession.

MIFFLIN, Pa., February 14.—Two weeks ago Geo. H. Wagner, a farmer, received a letter warning him that his property would be destroyed and he shot. No attention was paid to the matter. About 2 a. m. to-day his barn was fired in two places. Wagner ran out in his night clothes and a crowd of neighbors gathered. Shots were heard on the mountain and it was proposed to follow the incendias. Instead, the crowd stayed to save the property. The barn and contents were destroyed. Loss, $3,000. Hanged for Theft.
ATHENS, Ga., Feb. 14.—An account of one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record is just received from Guinnet County, this State, the victim of the mob's vengeance being a negro named Wm. Smeal, whose only crime was that of stealing horses. The negro was employed to work on the plantation of Mr. Tom Dillard, a prominent planter, and was said to be an industrious man, with a bad reputation, however, as a thief.

Some time last week a horse was stolen in the neighborhood, and suspicion was at once fixed upon the negro. So, upon Sunday night, a number of men organized themselves and resolved to inflict what they considered proper punishment upon the suspected man. They proceeded in a body to Mr. Dillard's place, broke open the cabin where the negro made his home, and carried him out.

They then took turns in beating the poor wretch until he confessed the theft and piloted the mob to where the stolen horse was tied up in the woods. But the negro's punishment did not end with this, as the mod at once procured a trace chain from a wagon, put it around the miserable man's neck and hanged him to a black-jack tree, near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville Road, where he was found hanging yesterday morning dead. There is much indignation over this atrocious act, and the perpetrators will be made to feel the law if they can be discovered.
